questions.question: What happens to the bread and wine in the Eucharist, and how is Christ present?
shared_ground: 'This is my body' and 'this is my blood' quoted or affirmed (excludes memorial, decides nothing among the other four)
Christ's body and blood are truly given or received in the Supper (shared by spiritual presence, sacramental union, real change, transubstantiation)
Calling the Eucharist the body and blood of Christ, or the bread of life (all realist positions)
The Supper must be received worthily; unworthy eating brings judgment
The Supper is done in remembrance of Christ's death (all five positions)
Christ's body is in heaven at the Father's right hand (all positions affirm the ascension)

positions.name: Memorial

defined.source: Huldrych Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles, Article 18 (1523)
defined.quote: the mass is not a sacrifice, but is a remembrance of the sacrifice and assurance of the salvation which Christ has given us.

defined.source: Baptist Faith and Message, Article VII (2000)
defined.quote: The Lord's Supper is a symbolic act of obedience whereby members of the church, through partaking of the bread and the fruit of the vine, memorialize the death of the Redeemer and anticipate His second coming.

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
defined.quote: a memorial of his suffering and death

positions.statement: The bread and wine are symbols that call Christ's death to mind; Christ's body and blood are neither present in them nor received through them.
positions.mark: The passage says the bread and wine only represent or remind of Christ's body and blood, and that nothing more than this remembrance is given in the rite.
positions.first_defined: Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles (1523); Baptist Faith and Message (1925, revised 2000)

positions.name: Spiritual presence

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 29.7 (1646)
defined.quote: the body and blood of Christ being then, not corporally or carnally, in, with, or under the bread and wine; yet, as really, but spiritually, present to the faith of believers in that ordinance

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXVIII (1571)
defined.quote: The Body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten, in the Supper, only after an heavenly and spiritual manner. And the mean whereby the Body of Christ is received and eaten in the Supper is Faith.

defined.source: Second London Baptist Confession, 30.7 (1689)
defined.quote: spiritually receive, and feed upon Christ crucified, and all the benefits of his death

defined.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: The body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten in the Supper, only after a heavenly and spiritual manner. And the mean whereby the body of Christ is received and eaten in the Supper is faith.

defined.source: Confession of Faith of the Evangelical United Brethren Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: partake of the body and blood of Christ in a spiritual manner until he comes

positions.statement: Believers truly receive Christ's body and blood in the Supper, but spiritually and by faith; the body is not in or under the bread, and unbelievers receive only the outward signs.
positions.mark: The passage says Christ's body is received only spiritually or by faith (not by the mouth), or that unbelievers who eat receive the sign but not the body.
positions.first_defined: Consensus Tigurinus (1549); Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571); Westminster Confession (1646)

positions.name: Sacramental union

defined.source: Augsburg Confession, Article X (1530)
defined.quote: Of the Supper of the Lord they teach that the Body and Blood of Christ are truly present, and are distributed to those who eat the Supper of the Lord

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration VII.35 (1577)
defined.quote: under the bread, with the bread, in the bread [the body of Christ is present and offered], are employed, is that by means of them the papistical transubstantiation may be rejected and the sacramental union of the unchanged essence of the bread and of the body of Christ indicated

positions.statement: Christ's true body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine in their essence, and are received by the mouth by all who eat, worthy or unworthy.
positions.mark: The passage says the bread remains bread (keeps its nature or substance) while Christ's true body is present with it or given with it.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession, Article X (1530); Formula of Concord, Article VII (1577)

positions.name: Real change, manner undefined

defined.source: Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, Epiclesis
defined.quote: And make this bread the precious Body of Your Christ. ... And that which is in this cup the precious Blood of Your Christ. ... Changing them by Your Holy Spirit.

defined.source: Longer Catechism of St Philaret of Moscow, q. 340 (1830s)
defined.quote: the word transubstantiation is not to be taken to define the manner in which the bread and wine are changed into the Body and Blood of the Lord; for this none can understand but God

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1375
defined.quote: It is by the conversion of the bread and wine into Christ's body and blood that Christ becomes present in this sacrament.

defined.source: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, The Faith of the Church (text by V. C. Samuel, 1970)
defined.quote: During the service of the Holy Liturgy, the bread turns into the true flesh of the Son of God and the wine into the true blood of the Son of God.

defined.source: Assyrian Church of the East, Diocese of California, FAQ
defined.quote: The elements of bread and wine are transformed in the eucharistic prayer, in a mystical way, by the unseen action of the Holy Spirit who operates through the priest celebrating this most sacred action.

positions.statement: By God's action at the consecration the bread and wine are changed into, and become, Christ's body and blood, so that they are no longer simply bread and wine; how the change happens is not defined.
positions.mark: The passage says the bread and wine are changed, transformed or made into Christ's body and blood (a change in what they are), without saying how.
positions.first_defined: Prayed in the eastern epiclesis; stated by the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) and, for Catholics, Lateran IV (1215) and Trent (1551)

first_uncertain.author: Cyril of Alexandria
first_uncertain.text: The Lord gives thanks when he takes the cup — that is, in the form of prayer he converses with God the Father, declaring him as it were sharer and co-approver of the life-giving blessing that will be given to us, and at the same time giving us a pattern first to give thanks and thus to break the bread and distribute it. positions.name: Transubstantiation

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 13, Canon 2 (1551)
defined.quote: that wonderful and singular conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the Body, and of the whole substance of the wine into the Blood-the species Only of the bread and wine remaining-which conversion indeed the Catholic Church most aptly calls Transubstantiation

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 13, ch. 1 (1551)
defined.quote: He be, in many other places, sacramentally present to us in his own substance, by a manner of existing, which, though we can scarcely express it in words

positions.statement: The whole substance of the bread and wine is converted into the substance of Christ's body and blood, while the appearances (everything the senses or any physical test can detect) remain; so the change is not physical or chemical.
positions.mark: The passage distinguishes what the bread is (now Christ's body) from what it still appears to be to the senses (bread), saying the appearance remains while the reality is changed.
positions.first_defined: Fourth Lateran Council (1215); Council of Trent, Session 13 (1551)

passages.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea
passages.text: Since the Spirit is the bread of the coming age, which is a food of life for the one approaching the age, and 'the bread which I will give' to you is 'my flesh for the life of the world' (John 6:51), and the blood is living in the body; and for this reason Moses said 'the life of all flesh' (Leviticus 17:11) regarding 'the blood' as being unified by blood. He clearly distinguished the type by the name of the truth, saying: 'this is my body'; and for this reason he named the types with the names of the truth, so that they would not be trivialized by what is seen, but would marvel at the power. Thus, eating and drinking showed the participation which would not have occurred without a body; for if the divine power had not been joined to a body and unified by blood, we would not have had communion through it to God.

memorial.quote: eating and drinking showed the participation which would not have occurred without a body; for if the divine power had not been joined to a body and unified by blood, we would not have had communion through it to God
memorial.audited: ATTRIBUTION: a catena fragment; the Greek opens 'τύπον δὲ ποιεῖ Ἀπολινάριος' ('Apollinaris makes [it] a type'), so a compiler is reporting him. It affirms 'this is my body' and says the types bear the names of the truth 'so that they would not be belittled for what is seen, but marvelled at for the power', which excludes a mere reminder. The English section omits the opening clause on 'participation in the body and blood accomplished in spirit for believers'.

passages.author: Evagrius Ponticus
passages.text: They wear away the flesh of Christ and squander the blood, regarding it as common; for he says, 'He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day' (John 6:54).

memorial.quote: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life

passages.author: Epiphanius of Salamis
passages.text: May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ—a divine body, a body that brings salvation to souls and bodies. And may what has been mixed in this cup into one reality become the blood of Christ, the blood of the new covenant, blood that brings salvation to us. Grant this so that we may wholly share in your mysteries in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter.

memorial.quote: May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ—a divine body, a body that brings salvation to souls and bodies

sacramental-union.quote: May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ

eucharistic-change.quote: May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ

passages.text: to the apostles, saying, “Take, eat; this is my body, which is being broken for you for the forgiveness of sins.” In the same way, after supper, he took the cup, having mixed it from two elements—from the fruit of the vine and water—sealed the cup of immortality, and gave it to his disciples, saying, “Drink from it, all of you; this is my blood of the new covenant, which is being poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins.”

memorial.quote: this is my body, which is being broken for you for the forgiveness of sins

passages.text: That Christ is life and life-giving. From the letter to the Corinthians: “I speak as to the wise; judge what I say. The cup of blessing that we bless — is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break — is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we the many are one body; for we all partake of the one bread.” (1 Corinthians 10:15–17) Human flesh, as far as its own nature goes, would not be life-giving, nor would human blood if it were common and by itself; but Christ’s body and precious blood give life — and being able to give life belongs to God alone…

passages.text: I myself receive by faith the flesh of the life-giving Word which gives life; therefore the Savior said, 'Those who eat from this bread will never taste death for eternity' (John 6:51); those who…

questions.question: Is the Eucharist a sacrifice, and if so, of what kind?
shared_ground: Christ's sacrifice on the cross was once for all and complete (all positions affirm this)
The Supper remembers or proclaims Christ's death
Thanksgiving and praise are offered at the Eucharist (praise and propitiatory positions both affirm it)
Calling the Eucharist an 'offering' or 'sacrifice' with no statement of what is offered or for what purpose (decides between no-sacrifice and the others only)
Malachi 1:11 'pure offering' applied to Christian worship without further specification

positions.name: Not a sacrifice

defined.source: Huldrych Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles, Article 18 (1523)
defined.quote: the mass is not a sacrifice, but is a remembrance of the sacrifice and assurance of the salvation which Christ has given us.

positions.statement: The Supper is a remembrance of Christ's once-for-all sacrifice and is not itself a sacrifice in any sense.
positions.mark: The passage says the Supper is not a sacrifice at all, only a remembrance.
positions.first_defined: Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles (1523)

positions.name: Sacrifice of praise and commemoration only

defined.source: Apology of the Augsburg Confession, XXIV.19 (1531)
defined.quote: The other species is the eucharistic sacrifice, which does not merit the remission of sins or reconciliation, but is rendered by those who have been reconciled, in order that we may give thanks

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 29.2 (1646)
defined.quote: In this sacrament, Christ is not offered up to his Father; nor any real sacrifice made at all, for remission of sins of the quick or dead; but only a commemoration of that one offering up of himself

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXXI (1571)
defined.quote: Wherefore the sacrifices of Masses, in the which it was commonly said, that the Priest did offer Christ for the quick and the dead, to have remission of pain or guilt, were blasphemous fables

positions.statement: The Supper includes a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving and commemorates Christ's sacrifice, but Christ is not offered to God in it and it obtains no forgiveness for the living or the dead.
positions.mark: The passage limits the Eucharistic offering to praise, thanksgiving or remembrance, denying that Christ is offered or that it obtains forgiveness for anyone.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession XXIV and Apology XXIV (1530-31); Thirty-Nine Articles XXXI (1563/71); Westminster 29.2 (1646)

positions.name: Propitiatory sacrifice

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 22, ch. 2 (1562)
defined.quote: that same Christ is contained and immolated in an unbloody manner, who once offered Himself in a bloody manner on the altar of the cross

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 17 (1672)
defined.quote: it is a true and propitiatory Sacrifice offered for all Orthodox, living and dead

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1367
defined.quote: The sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice

defined.source: CopticChurch.net, Sacraments: Eucharist
defined.quote: Be well knowledgeable of the sublime value of the sacrifice between your hands. He is Christ Emmanuel who sacrificed Himself for you.

positions.statement: In the Eucharist the one sacrifice of Christ is offered to God without bloodshed, and it obtains mercy and forgiveness for the living and the dead.
positions.mark: The passage says the Eucharist is offered for sins, or for the living and the dead to obtain mercy, or that Christ (his body and blood) is the victim offered in it.

first_states.author: Cyril of Alexandria
first_states.text: Cyril: So then the matter is fruit-bearing, O Palladius, and a mystical word has also been woven for it, I think, carrying the riddle up unto Emmanuel, and unto us ourselves; and I will speak again as I am able. For when the holy and true tent has been shown in this world—that is, the Church—Christ conspicuous in it many-formedly and all but from us and for us is brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father, a ransom and exchange of the life of all, one worth-all. And being one also himself, he was being written according to many manners, as at least in the bringing-for

no-sacrifice.quote: Christ conspicuous in it many-formedly and all but from us and for us is brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father
no-sacrifice.audited: Kept. 'Christ will be brought forward toward us and for us, being sacrificed mystically in the holy tents' (Greek μυστικῶς ἱερουργούμενος ἐν ταῖς ἁγίαις σκηναῖς), with a daily offering in the Church.

sacrifice-of-praise.quote: brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father, a ransom and exchange of the life of all
sacrifice-of-praise.audited: Kept. In the Church 'Christ ... from us and for us is brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father' (Greek ὡς ἱερὸν προσάγεται θύμα τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρί), so Christ himself is offered.

propitiatory-sacrifice.quote: Christ ... is brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father, a ransom and exchange of the life of all
propitiatory-sacrifice.audited: Kept. Christ is named as the victim offered in the churches, 'from us and for us ... a sacred victim to God and Father, a ransom and exchange of the life of all', and 'being sacrificed mystically in the holy tents' daily; Greek checked and faithful (ὡς ἱερὸν προσάγεται θύμα; μυστικῶς ἱερουργούμενος). Note the first clause carries Cyril's hedge μονονουχί ('all but'); the later clause does not.

passages.author: Origen of Alexandria
passages.text: With God permitting, then, and secondly the bishops, and thirdly the presbyters and the people too, I will speak again of what is stirring me at this point. The offering is always made to God Almighty through Jesus Christ, as offering his divinity to the Father. Let the offering not be made twice, but to God through God.

no-sacrifice.quote: The offering is always made to God Almighty through Jesus Christ, as offering his divinity to the Father.
no-sacrifice.audited: Kept. In a liturgical setting (bishops, presbyters, people) Origen says 'the offering is always made to God Almighty through Jesus Christ' (Greek Ἀεὶ προσφορὰ γίνεται Θεῷ παντοκράτορι διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ), calling the eucharistic prosphora an offering to God; the English is faithful. The year given is Origen's death; the Dialogue dates c. 245.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Cyril: …for we approach the holy things, for no other grace, than so as to share the holy Christ through the unspeakable and spiritual sacrifice. And the vessels serving the sacrifices are also thoroughly cleansed, so that they may not become for some other, nor may the things having liturgized for the sacred be carried under to humans’ needs. And the law has been kept, and is saved in churches. And that being blessed is fitting for those playing-the-man, the law will clarify again saying: ‘Every male among the priests will eat them.’ (Leviticus 6:30)

questions.question: What authority does the bishop of Rome hold over the whole Church?
shared_ground: Peter was a leading apostle, named first in the lists
Peter and Paul taught and died in Rome; Rome is an apostolic church
Rome is an important church whose faith is praised
Communion between churches, including with Rome, matters
Bishops succeed the apostles in their sees

positions.name: No special authority

defined.source: Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope, 9 (1537)
defined.quote: Christ sends forth His disciples on an equality, without any distinction

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXXVII (1571)
defined.quote: The Bishop of Rome hath no jurisdiction in this Realm of England

defined.source: Second London Baptist Confession, 26.4 (1689)
defined.quote: neither can the Pope of Rome in any sense be head thereof

positions.statement: The bishop of Rome holds no authority or rank over other churches by divine institution; all ministers are equal.
positions.mark: The passage says the apostles or bishops are all equal and that none, including Rome's, holds a God-given rank or authority over others.

positions.name: Primacy of honour among equals

defined.source: Moscow Patriarchate, Position on the problem of primacy in the Universal Church (2013)
defined.quote: In the first millennium of church history, the primacy of honour used to belong to the chair of Rome.

defined.source: Moscow Patriarchate, Position on the problem of primacy in the Universal Church (2013)
defined.quote: They also believed that primacy in honour accorded to the bishops of Rome is instituted not by God but men.

positions.statement: Rome held first place in honour among the churches, granted by the Church and not by divine right, without jurisdiction over other local churches.
positions.mark: The passage gives Rome first rank or precedence while denying it jurisdiction over other churches, or grounds its rank in councils or the city rather than in Christ's grant to Peter.
positions.first_defined: Councils of Constantinople (381, canon 3) and Chalcedon (451, canon 28) on the order of sees; Moscow Patriarchate statement (2013)

positions.name: Primacy of jurisdiction by divine right

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 2 (1870)
defined.quote: Therefore whoever succeeds to the chair of Peter obtains by the institution of Christ himself, the primacy of Peter over the whole church.

defined.source: Council of Florence, Laetentur Caeli (1439)
defined.quote: to him was committed in blessed Peter the full power of tending, ruling and governing the whole church

positions.statement: By Christ's institution, the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor holds full and immediate power to govern the whole Church.
positions.mark: The passage says Rome's bishop, as Peter's successor, has authority (not only honour) over all churches, such as to judge, depose or bind other bishops, by Christ's grant.
positions.first_defined: Council of Florence (1439); First Vatican Council (1870)

positions.name: Infallibility of solemn papal definitions

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)
defined.quote: when the Roman pontiff speaks EX CATHEDRA, that is, when, in the exercise of his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole church, he possesses ... that infallibility which the divine Redeemer willed his church to enjoy

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)
defined.quote: such definitions of the Roman pontiff are of themselves, and not by the consent of the church, irreformable.

positions.statement: When the bishop of Rome solemnly defines a doctrine of faith or morals for the whole Church, he cannot err, and the definition binds without the Church's later consent.
positions.mark: The passage says a Roman bishop's doctrinal decision cannot be in error, or is final in itself without needing a council's or the churches' acceptance.
positions.first_defined: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)

questions.question: May Mary be called Mother of God (Theotokos)?
shared_ground: Mary is the mother of Jesus
Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit of the virgin Mary
Mary did not give the Word his divine nature

positions.name: Mother of God (Theotokos)

defined.source: Council of Ephesus, Cyril's First Anathema (431)
defined.quote: If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is God in truth, and therefore that the holy virgin is the mother of God

defined.source: Council of Chalcedon, Definition of Faith (451)
defined.quote: in the last days the same for us and for our salvation from Mary, the virgin God-bearer as regards his humanity

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), The Holy Virgin Saint Mary
defined.quote: She is, in the belief of the Church, the mother of God, (Theotokos in Coptic)

positions.statement: Because the one born of Mary is God the Word made flesh, Mary is rightly called Mother of God.
positions.mark: The passage calls Mary Mother of God or God-bearer, or says God was born of her.
positions.first_defined: Council of Ephesus (431); Council of Chalcedon (451)

first_states.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea (quoted as Athanasius)
first_states.text: So the one born from the holy virgin is Son of God by nature and true God, not by grace and sharing. Only according to the flesh from Mary is he human; according to the Spirit he himself is Son of God and God.

theotokos.audited: 'the one born from the holy virgin is Son of God by nature and true God, not by grace' says God was born of her, which is the mark. ATTRIBUTION: Cyril quotes this as Athanasius, but the source is the pseudo-Athanasian creed to Jovian, really by Apollinaris of Laodicea (c. 363); the words are not Cyril's and the 444 date is wrong for them.

christotokos.quote: the one born from the holy virgin is Son of God by nature and true God
christotokos.audited: 'the one born from the holy virgin is ... true God, not by grace and sharing' says God was born of her. positions.name: Mother of Christ only
positions.statement: Mary should be called mother of Christ, not Mother of God, because she bore the humanity, not the Godhead.
positions.mark: The passage refuses the title Mother of God, preferring mother of Christ or of the man.
positions.first_defined: Condemned at Ephesus (431)

first_uncertain.author: Nestorius (as quoted)
first_uncertain.text: Nestorius says: When the divine Scripture speaks of the birth of Christ from Mary the virgin, it nowhere appears as God, but as Christ or the Lord Jesus, because these three terms are significant of the two natures, now referring to one, now to the other; I mean: When the birth from the Virgin is announced to us of Christ, the Apostle says, 'God sent his Son, born of a woman'; he did not say, 'Sent God the Word'; but he takes the name indicating the two births, namely God and man, because Christ is double; for the Virgin bore a Son of God, as he breathed; but you are gods and sons of the Most High all, whence we learned to say Christotokos, Kyriotokos, anthropotokos from Scripture, but we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos, that is, God-bearer or Mother of God.

theotokos.quote: we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos, that is, God-bearer or Mother of God
theotokos.audited: Nestorius's words: 'we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos'. Greek confirmed: 'Θεοτόκον δὲ οὐδαμῶς ἐδιδάχθημεν λέγειν τὴν ἁγίαν Παρθένον'. ATTRIBUTION: these are Nestorius's words, not Cyril's, and the Dialogue with Nestorius is widely treated as not by Cyril; credit them to Nestorius (c. 428-431).

christotokos.quote: we learned to say Christotokos, Kyriotokos, anthropotokos from Scripture, but we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos, that is, God-bearer or Mother of God
christotokos.audited: 'we learned to say Christotokos, Kyriotokos, anthropotokos ... but never ... Theotokos' (Χριστοτόκον ... Θεοτόκον δὲ οὐδαμῶς) is the mark: it refuses Mother of God and prefers mother of Christ. ATTRIBUTION: the speaker is Nestorius; the dialogue's ascription to Cyril is doubtful.

first_uncertain.attribution_note: Nestorius' words, quoted in a dialogue whose ascription to Cyril is doubted.

passages.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea (quoted as Athanasius)
passages.text: So the one born from the holy virgin is Son of God by nature and true God, not by grace and sharing. Only according to the flesh from Mary is he human; according to the Spirit he himself is Son of God and God.

passages.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea (quoted as Athanasius)
passages.text: — worshiped, and worshiped with his flesh in one worship. Not two sons: one a true Son of God who is worshiped, and another a human from Mary who is not worshiped, made a son of God by grace as humans are. But the one from God, as I said — one Son of God and God, himself and no other — also born from Mary according to the flesh in the last days, as the angel said to the God-bearer Mary when she asked, “How will this be, since I do not know a man?” — “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who is born will be called Son of God.” (Luke 1:34–35)

theotokos.quote: as the angel said to the God-bearer Mary
theotokos.audited: 'as the angel said to the God-bearer Mary'; Greek 'τῇ θεοτόκῳ Μαρίᾳ' confirmed. ATTRIBUTION: Cyril quotes this as Athanasius, but the source is the pseudo-Athanasian creed to Jovian, really by Apollinaris of Laodicea (c. 363); the words are not Cyril's and the 444 date is wrong for them.

christotokos.quote: as the angel said to the God-bearer Mary
christotokos.audited: 'the God-bearer Mary' (τῇ θεοτόκῳ Μαρίᾳ), with 'one Son of God and God ... born from Mary according to the flesh'. passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: 27.17 But Isaiah cries out to Him without comparison as the God the Father: 'From eternity we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen a God besides You' (Isa 64:4). 27.18 For we saw no other God than the one born according to the saving incarnation from the Virgin Mary, nor did we hear [of any] except the one attested by God the Father: 27.19 'This is my beloved Son' (Matt 3:17).

theotokos.quote: we saw no other God than the one born according to the saving incarnation from the Virgin Mary
theotokos.audited: 'we saw no other God than the one born ... from the Virgin Mary'; Greek 'θεὸν ἢ τὸν ἐκ παρθένου Μαρίας ... τεχθέντα' confirmed. God was born of her. ATTRIBUTION: De Trinitate's ascription to Didymus is disputed by modern scholars; treat the 398 date as doubtful.

christotokos.quote: we saw no other God than the one born according to the saving incarnation from the Virgin Mary
christotokos.audited: 'no other God than the one born ... from the Virgin Mary' (θεὸν ... ἐκ παρθένου Μαρίας ... τεχθέντα) says God was born of her. ATTRIBUTION: De Trinitate's ascription to Didymus is disputed.

passages.attribution_note: Attribution of De Trinitate to Didymus is disputed.

passages.author: John Chrysostom (quoted by Cyril)
passages.text: From John, bishop of Constantinople, on the divine birth. He says of the holy virgin: “Instead of a sun, he says, she contains without limit the sun of righteousness. Nature’s order is overcome; for he willed, he was able, he came down, he saved — all things run together for God. Today the One who is is born, and the One who is becomes what he was not. Being God, he becomes human without leaving off being God. He did not become human by departing from deity, nor become God by climbing up from humanity. Being Word, he became flesh without suffering change; his nature remained unchanged.” (Malachi 4:2) He adds: “He who sits on a high and lifted throne is laid in a manger. The untouchable, simple, bodiless one is wrapped by human hands. He who breaks the bonds of sin is tangled in swaddling cloths.” (Isaiah 6:1)

christotokos.quote: Being God, he becomes human without leaving off being God. He did not become human by departing from deity
christotokos.audited: Borderline but met: said 'of the holy virgin', 'Today the One who is is born ... Being God, he becomes human' says God was born of her. ATTRIBUTION: Cyril quotes these as John Chrysostom 'on the divine birth'; they are not Cyril's words, and the Chrysostom ascription should be checked.

passages.attribution_note: Quoted by Cyril as Chrysostom; the ascription still needs checking.

passages.author: Antiochus of Ptolemais (quoted by Cyril)
passages.text: From bishop Antiochus: “For yesterday, in undefiled birth pangs, the life-bearer, the fair-bearer, the great-bearer, the light-bearer, the hope-bearer, the God-bearer, the strange-bearer, the virgin-mother Mary brought us a Savior.” (John 1:14)

theotokos.quote: the God-bearer, the virgin-mother Mary brought us a Savior
theotokos.audited: 'the God-bearer ... Mary'; Greek 'ἡ θεοτόκος' confirmed in the list of titles. ATTRIBUTION: these are Antiochus of Ptolemais's words (d. c. 408) quoted by Cyril, not Cyril's own.

christotokos.quote: the God-bearer, the virgin-mother Mary brought us a Savior
christotokos.audited: Calls Mary 'the God-bearer' (ἡ θεοτόκος), which excludes mother-of-Christ-only. Words are Antiochus of Ptolemais's, quoted by Cyril.

passages.author: Severian of Gabala (quoted by Cyril)
passages.text: From bishop Severianus: “For the Word begotten from above from the Father — beyond speech, beyond telling, beyond grasp, eternally — is himself begotten in time from below from the virgin Mary, so that those first born from below may be born from above from a second birth, that is, from God.” (John 3:3–7)

theotokos.quote: the Word ... is himself begotten in time ... from the virgin Mary
theotokos.audited: 'the Word begotten from above from the Father ... is himself begotten in time from below from the virgin Mary': the Word is born of her. Greek 'ὁ αὐτὸς ἐν χρόνῳ γεννᾶται κάτωθεν ἐκ παρθένου Μαρίας' confirmed. ATTRIBUTION: Severian of Gabala's words (d. after 408), quoted by Cyril.

christotokos.quote: the Word ... is himself begotten in time ... from the virgin Mary
christotokos.audited: 'the Word ... is himself (ὁ αὐτός) begotten in time ... from the virgin Mary' says God the Word was born of her. Words are Severian of Gabala's, quoted by Cyril.

passages.author: Ammonius of Adrianople (quoted by Cyril)
passages.text: From Ammonius, bishop of Adrianople: “For he too said somewhere about the Word of God: But if he himself is God by nature, as God’s Only-begotten Son, and in taking the slave’s form was also counted worthy to be called firstborn son of the holy virgin, he gave himself as a ransom for all.” He goes on: “I have already shown the impiety into which the Arians fall when they say the God-bearer Mary needed the sacrifices then offered under the law for women who give birth.”

theotokos.audited: 'the God-bearer Mary'; Greek 'τὴν θεοτόκον Μαρίαν' confirmed. ATTRIBUTION: Ammonius of Adrianople's words, quoted by Cyril, not Cyril's own.

christotokos.quote: the God-bearer Mary
christotokos.audited: Calls her 'the God-bearer Mary' (θεοτόκον Μαρίαν). Words are Ammonius of Adrianople's, quoted by Cyril.

passages.text: Nestorius says: When the divine Scripture speaks of the birth of Christ from Mary the virgin, it nowhere appears as God, but as Christ or the Lord Jesus, because these three terms are significant of the two natures, now referring to one, now to the other; I mean: When the birth from the Virgin is announced to us of Christ, the Apostle says, 'God sent his Son, born of a woman'; he did not say, 'Sent God the Word'; but he takes the name indicating the two births, namely God and man, because Christ is double; for the Virgin bore a Son of God, as he breathed; but you are gods and sons of the Most High all, whence we learned to say Christotokos, Kyriotokos, anthropotokos from Scripture, but we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos, that is, God-bearer or Mother of God.

theotokos.audited: Nestorius's words: 'we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos'. Greek confirmed: 'Θεοτόκον δὲ οὐδαμῶς ἐδιδάχθημεν λέγειν τὴν ἁγίαν Παρθένον'. christotokos.audited: 'we learned to say Christotokos, Kyriotokos, anthropotokos ... but never ... Theotokos' (Χριστοτόκον ... passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: From Luke. “And it came to pass while they were there that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her son, the firstborn, and wrapped him and laid him in the manger, because there was no place for them in the lodging.” (Luke 2:6–7) The holy virgin has borne one and only son, Emmanuel. How then does it say “her son, the firstborn” (Romans 8:29)? For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin. So it is marked from the God-breathed scripture: the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn. For he has shared blood and flesh and similarly to us shared the same things. Thus he became firstborn among many brothers; yet as God he is worshiped by us ourselves and by the spirits above.

theotokos.quote: the holy virgin has borne ... the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn
theotokos.audited: Borderline but met: 'The holy virgin has borne one and only son, Emmanuel ... the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn' identifies her firstborn son with the Only-begotten Word, so the Word was born of her. Greek 'μόνον τέτοκεν υἱὸν τὸν Ἐμμανουὴλ ἡ ἁγία παρθένος' confirmed.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: If the church belongs to God and Christ has presented it to himself, then it is clear that God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary.

theotokos.quote: God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary
theotokos.audited: 'God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary': calls her God-bearing and says God came from her.

christotokos.quote: God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary
christotokos.audited: 'God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary' says God was born of her.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: We say that this same Only-begotten Word, begotten beyond speech from the substance of God the Father, maker of the ages, the one through whom and in whom all things are, the true light, the nature that gives life to all — for he has appeared as life from the Father’s life — in the last times of the age, when the Father was pleased to save the race on earth that had fallen under a curse and been brought down by sin into death and decay, took hold of Abraham’s seed, as the Scriptures say, shared blood and flesh — that is, became human — and taking flesh and making it his own, was born in the flesh through the holy God-bearer Mary (Hebrews 2:16).

theotokos.quote: was born in the flesh through the holy God-bearer Mary
theotokos.audited: 'was born in the flesh through the holy God-bearer Mary'; Greek 'διὰ τῆς ἁγίας καὶ θεοτόκου Μαρίας' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: was born in the flesh through the holy God-bearer Mary
christotokos.audited: 'the holy God-bearer Mary' (θεοτόκου Μαρίας) uses the title the position refuses.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: But the word God-bearer was already customary even with the holy fathers before us, who are admired for right faith, and still with all under heaven, so to speak. I thought I had to declare that as true.

theotokos.quote: the word God-bearer was already customary even with the holy fathers before us
theotokos.audited: 'the word God-bearer was already customary even with the holy fathers ... I thought I had to declare that as true': Cyril affirms the title.

christotokos.quote: I thought I had to declare that as true
christotokos.audited: Affirming 'the word God-bearer' as true and customary rules out refusing it.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: But we do say this: look — all the best and wisest fathers of our times also name the holy virgin God-bearer, and they affirm that the Word from God has been united by nature to the flesh, that he came to be in the virgin’s womb, and that he came forth from her according to the flesh.

theotokos.quote: all the best and wisest fathers of our times also name the holy virgin God-bearer
theotokos.audited: 'all the best and wisest fathers of our times also name the holy virgin God-bearer'; Greek 'θεοτόκον ὀνομάζουσι τὴν ἁγίαν παρθένον' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: all the best and wisest fathers of our times also name the holy virgin God-bearer
christotokos.audited: Endorses naming the virgin 'God-bearer' (θεοτόκον), the title the position refuses.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: For the Son from God the Father by nature, taking to himself an ensouled and intelligent body, has been begotten according to the flesh through the holy virgin and Theotokos Mary — not turned into flesh (far from it!), but rather taking it on, and not neglecting to be God.

theotokos.quote: through the holy virgin and Theotokos Mary
theotokos.audited: 'begotten according to the flesh through the holy virgin and Theotokos Mary'; Greek 'διὰ τῆς ἁγίας παρθένου καὶ θεοτόκου Μαρίας' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: through the holy virgin and Theotokos Mary
christotokos.audited: Uses 'Theotokos' (θεοτόκου Μαρίας) as her title.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: — not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself enfleshed, with a body from her as his own. That is why he is said to have been begotten in the flesh: he makes the begetting of his own flesh his.

theotokos.quote: not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself enfleshed, with a body from her as his own
theotokos.audited: 'not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself enfleshed ... he is said to have been begotten in the flesh': the Word was born of her.

christotokos.quote: not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself enfleshed
christotokos.audited: 'not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself' rejects 'she bore only a man' directly.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Those who senselessly deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer are forced to say there are two sons of God. For if she did not bear in the flesh the enfleshed God, they must admit — willing or not — that she bore only a common human, with nothing more than we have.

theotokos.quote: Those who senselessly deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer are forced to say there are two sons of God
theotokos.audited: 'Those who senselessly deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer'; Greek 'θεοτόκον οὐκ εἶναι τὴν ἁγίαν παρθένον' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: Those who senselessly deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer
christotokos.audited: Condemns those who 'deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer', which is the christotokos position itself.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: So if they say that the one born from the holy virgin is true God — that is, the Word from God the Father united by nature to flesh — why do they fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer?

theotokos.quote: why do they fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer?
theotokos.audited: 'why do they fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer?': urges the title outright.

christotokos.quote: why do they fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer?
christotokos.audited: Rebukes those who 'fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer'.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: In the same breath he sets down two things proper to God, and not fitting for human nature. Of the one born from Mary he said that those saved through him are his own people, and that he himself will also free them from sins. All things belong to God, and to him alone it would befit to be able to free sinners from sins. So the one begotten from the holy virgin is God, whose own people we are; and he has freed us from sins, as one who has authority for that too.

theotokos.quote: So the one begotten from the holy virgin is God, whose own people we are
theotokos.audited: 'So the one begotten from the holy virgin is God': God was born of her.

christotokos.quote: So the one begotten from the holy virgin is God, whose own people we are
christotokos.audited: 'the one begotten from the holy virgin is God' says God was born of her.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Since he emptied himself by becoming in the likeness of a man, and was found in the form of a man, he receives the common name, that is, Christ and Jesus, or rather, Emmanuel. The name Emmanuel signifies 'God with us.' For it is written, 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel' (Isaiah 7:14). For the blessed Gabriel revealed the mystery to the holy and God-bearing virgin, saying, 'Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with God, and behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he shall save his people from their sins' (Matthew 1:21-23). Are the prophet and the blessed angel inconsistent with one another? Not at all. For the blessed prophet speaks mysteries by the Spirit, having foretold a God who has become with us, naming him so both from his nature and from the economy of the flesh.

theotokos.audited: 'the holy and God-bearing virgin': Cyril calls her God-bearer.

passages.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
passages.text: Therefore, even that which is being born shall be called the holy Son of God. Do you see how immense the dignity of the Mother of God is, being a virgin.

theotokos.quote: Do you see how immense the dignity of the Mother of God is, being a virgin.
theotokos.audited: 'Do you see how immense the dignity of the Mother of God is'; Greek 'τὸ τῆς θεοτόκου παρθένου ... ἀξίωμα' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: Do you see how immense the dignity of the Mother of God is, being a virgin.
christotokos.audited: Calls her the Theotokos virgin (τῆς θεοτόκου παρθένου).

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 499
defined.quote: The deepening of faith in the virginal motherhood led the Church to confess Mary's real and perpetual virginity even in the act of giving birth to the Son of God made man.

passages.text: In that [passage]: 'Father, if it is possible.' Again, like a lawful soldier, I take up the fight against the heretics, with Stephen, the commander of piety, leading the ranks. For just as Jesus was turning the enemies when Moses was praying, so also I, with the martyr cooperating, lay hold of the enemies of the truth. I say these things not daring through an abundance of words, but having trusted in the prayer of the martyr, I dare to speak these words. For I do not fear their bulk in words. I fear the obstacles of their bad-crafty deception. For we learned not to fear a fear that did not exist.

commemoration-only.quote: having trusted in the prayer of the martyr, I dare to speak these words
commemoration-only.audited: 'Having trusted in the prayer of the martyr (τῇ προσευχῇ τοῦ μάρτυρος πεποιθώς)' Stephen, with 'the martyr cooperating', says a departed saint prays for the living speaker.

passages.author: Asterius of Amasea
passages.text: For our prayer is not sufficient to move God in the time of necessity or misfortune, for our plea is not a persuasion, but a remembrance of sins; therefore we fly to the fellow-servants who are loved by the Lord, so that they might heal our defects through their own achievements. first_uncertain.author: Severianus of Gabala
first_uncertain.text: The Savior, having received this voice, says: 'Today salvation has come to this house' (Luke 19:9). He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ. Today salvation has come to this house, because this man also is a son of Abraham. Before doing the works of Abraham, he does not call him a son of Abraham, but calls him Zacchaeus by the bare appellation; but when he fulfilled the works of the patriarch, promising charity and the restitution of the injustice, then he says: 'And this man also is a son of Abraham.'

forensic-imputation.quote: He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ
forensic-imputation.audited: 'He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ' (Αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν ἐδικαίωσεν... ἐπειδὴ τοῖς Χριστοῦ ὑπήκουσε νόμοις); salvation comes when he 'fulfilled the works of the patriarch'. Greek checked: faithful. Justification by obedience rules out faith-alone imputation. Borderline: homiletic, playing on his self-condemnation just before.

infused-righteousness.quote: He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ
infused-righteousness.audited: Zacchaeus is justified 'because he obeyed the laws of Christ', and the sermon continues 'let us adorn faith with works' (σεμνύνωμεν τοῖς ἔργοις τὴν πίστιν). That is justification by faith together with works. Borderline: a preacher's point, not a definition. passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: He might pass from one [state] to another. If he had not become one in the truth, not standing in it would not have brought him reproach. And behold the doctrine: how 'God wants all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth' (1 Tim 2:4)? If no one opposes His will, how is it that some are lagging behind, despite His wanting all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth—so that I may not say, the majority? If He wants [it], and if we also want [it], and a convergence of the two wills occurs, salvation happens; for no one is good against his will, no one who does not want is saved, and no one hurrying toward approaching God and having kept His law is able to know the truth.

double.quote: no one is good against his will, no one who does not want is saved
double.audited: 'God wants all men to be saved', and salvation needs 'a convergence of the two wills'. This fits the double position's own exclusion clause: he wills all to be saved.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: Again, concerning Esau and Jacob, the apostle, as if speaking in a dilemma, says: 'What then shall we say to this? Is there injustice with God? May it never be!' (Romans 9:14). Because he had refuted injustice, he forced us to seek how there is not injustice with God. If it were so, as those who speak of foreknowledge say, we would rather find injustice in Him. 'I loved Jacob,' He says, 'but I hated Esau' (Romans 9:13). But one is hated or loved according to things done and according to things thought. How then does foreknowledge have room? Is injustice found with God? But he, refuting this, said: 'What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? May it never be!' Since there is no injustice, let the matter be sought in another way, how it has come to pass.

foreknowledge.quote: If it were so, as those who speak of foreknowledge say, we would rather find injustice in Him
foreknowledge.audited: 'If it were as those who speak of foreknowledge say, we would rather find injustice with Him... How then does foreknowledge have room?' (πῶς οὖν χώραν ἔχει ἡ πρόγνωσις;). Greek checked: faithful. Didymus rejects foreknowledge as the basis and grounds love and hate in things actually done and thought. That is not an unconditional decree, so it gives no support to 'double'.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: But did Paul speak according to foreknowledge? Foreknowledge is a theoretical viewing of what is coming to be. But according to kind, foreknowledge and knowledge are the same. They differ in time. For example, suppose I foreknow that tomorrow there will be thunder. When the thunder comes to be in the middle of the day, it is knowledge, no longer foreknowledge. And the knowledge of the thunder does not make it such, but what it is, that becomes the knowledge. Thus the known thing makes the knowledge, which does not receive the knowing from us. I use an image for the sake of the manner of foreknowledge: the one [child] is born so that he may demand, and the other, so that he may live in the house. What kind of justice is this of foreknowledge, if we take these things to happen according to foreknowledge? Foreknowledge both justifies and condemns. To foreknow and to know is also to condemn

foreknowledge.quote: the known thing makes the knowledge, which does not receive the knowing from us
foreknowledge.audited: 'What kind of justice is this of foreknowledge, if we take these things to happen according to foreknowledge?' (Greek checked) begins Didymus' rejection of the foreknowledge account, completed in d57e3d085a87fe48 ('How then does foreknowledge have room?').

questions.question: Do gifts such as tongues, prophecy and healing continue in the Church today, and is speaking in tongues the sign of a baptism in the Spirit?
shared_ground: The Holy Spirit gives gifts to the Church (1 Corinthians 12)
Love is greater than any gift (1 Corinthians 13)
Gifts are for building up the Church
Miracles were done by the apostles (as history)
The Spirit was poured out at Pentecost with tongues (Acts 2 retold)

positions.name: Baptism in the Spirit, first shown by tongues

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
defined.quote: This experience is distinct from and subsequent to the experience of the new birth.

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
defined.quote: The baptism of believers in the Holy Spirit is witnessed by the initial physical sign of speaking with other tongues as the Spirit of God gives them utterance.

defined.source: Church of God (Cleveland, TN), Declaration of Faith
defined.quote: In speaking with other tongues as the Spirit gives utterance and that it is the initial evidence of the baptism in the Holy Ghost.

positions.statement: After conversion believers should seek a further baptism in the Holy Spirit, whose first outward sign is speaking in tongues; all the gifts named in 1 Corinthians 12 continue.
positions.mark: The passage says believers receive the Spirit in a distinct experience after faith, and that speaking in tongues is the sign that they have received it.
positions.first_defined: Charles Parham's 'Bible evidence' teaching (Topeka, 1901); Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916)

positions.name: Gifts continue as the Spirit gives them

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2003
defined.quote: Whatever their character - sometimes it is extraordinary, such as the gift of miracles or of tongues - charisms are oriented toward sanctifying grace

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 799-801
defined.quote: No charism is exempt from being referred and submitted to the Church's shepherds.

defined.source: UMC Book of Resolutions, Guidelines: The UMC and the Charismatic Movement
defined.quote: their charismatic gifts and experiences can be considered as fresh wind of the Spirit

defined.source: UMC Book of Resolutions, Guidelines: The UMC and the Charismatic Movement
defined.quote: When United Methodist charismatics adopt a classical pentecostal line, they are no longer United Methodist-at least in the Wesleyan sense.

defined.source: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995)
defined.quote: We know from Scripture that the Holy Spirit continues to reveal God's will to us (1 Cor. 14:26-33).

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), Comparative Theology (1988)
defined.quote: God endows whatever gift He wishes to whomever He wishes in the time His Divine Wisdom defines

positions.statement: The Spirit still gives gifts such as healing, prophecy and tongues as he wills; no single gift is the required sign of having the Spirit, and gifts are tested by the Church.
positions.mark: The passage says gifts such as prophecy, healing, miracles or tongues are still given in the writer's own day, and says or implies that not every Spirit-filled believer speaks in tongues.
positions.first_defined: No single defining text; Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992), paragraphs 799-801 and 2003; UMC Guidelines on the Charismatic Movement (1976)

positions.name: New revelation ceased with the apostles

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith (1646)
defined.quote: those former ways of God's revealing his will unto his people being now ceased.

defined.source: Second London Baptist Confession (1689), ch. 1
defined.quote: those former ways of God's revealing his will unto his people being now ceased.

positions.statement: God's former ways of giving new revelation, such as prophecy and tongues as revelation, ended with the apostles once Scripture was complete; such revelation is not given today.
positions.mark: The passage says new revelation, through prophecy or tongues, ended with the apostles or is no longer given.
positions.first_defined: Westminster Confession 1.1 (1646); Second London Baptist Confession 1.1 (1689)

questions.question: Can a Christian be made wholly holy in this life, and when is sanctification made complete?
shared_ground: Believers are called to holiness ('be holy, for I am holy')
Sanctification is God's work by the Spirit
Growth in grace through life
Exhortations to be perfect (Matthew 5:48) without saying perfection is reached
The souls of the righteous are made perfect at death (shared by both positions that deny purification after death)

positions.name: Entire sanctification in this life

defined.source: Confession of Faith of the Evangelical United Brethren Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: Entire sanctification is a state of perfect love, righteousness and true holiness which every regenerate believer may obtain by being delivered from the power of sin

defined.source: Confession of Faith of the Evangelical United Brethren Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: Through faith in Jesus Christ this gracious gift may be received in this life both gradually and instantaneously

defined.source: Church of the Nazarene, Articles of Faith (Manual 2023)
defined.quote: We believe that entire sanctification is that act of God, subsequent to regeneration, by which believers are made free from original sin, or depravity

defined.source: International Pentecostal Holiness Church, Articles of Faith
defined.quote: we believe it includes a definite, instantaneous work of grace achieved by faith subsequent to regeneration

defined.source: Church of God (Cleveland, TN), Declaration of Faith
defined.quote: In sanctification subsequent to the new birth, through faith in the blood of Christ; through the Word, and by the Holy Ghost.

positions.statement: After regeneration God can, by a further work received through faith, free the believer from the power of sin and make him perfect in love in this life; growth in grace continues afterwards.
positions.mark: The passage says a believer can be made wholly holy, free from sin's power or perfect in love, in this life, as a work of God after conversion.
positions.first_defined: Methodist Protestant article on sanctification, placed in the Methodist Discipline (1939); John Wesley's teaching on Christian perfection (18th century, not itself a church confession); EUB Confession XI; Nazarene Articles of Faith

positions.name: Progressive, made complete at death

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith (1646)
defined.quote: This sanctification is throughout, in the whole man; yet imperfect in this life, there abiding still some remnants of corruption in every part

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith (1646)
defined.quote: the souls of the righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens

defined.source: Second London Baptist Confession (1689), ch. 13
defined.quote: This sanctification is throughout the whole man, yet imperfect in this life

defined.source: Baptist Faith and Message (2000)
defined.quote: Growth in grace should continue throughout the regenerate person's life.

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles (1571)
defined.quote: But all we the rest, although baptized, and born again in Christ, yet offend in many things; and if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Epitome (1577)
defined.quote: notwithstanding the fact that many weaknesses and defects cling to the true believers and truly regenerate, even to the grave

positions.statement: Sanctification begins at regeneration and grows through life but stays incomplete; remaining sin is removed only at death, when the soul is made perfect in holiness.
positions.mark: The passage says even the regenerate stay imperfect or keep sinning until death.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession (1530) and Formula of Concord (1577); Thirty-Nine Articles XV (1563/1571); Westminster Confession 13 and 32 (1646)

positions.name: Completed by purification after death if not in this life

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1030-1031
defined.quote: All who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, are indeed assured of their eternal salvation; but after death they undergo purification, so as to achieve the holiness necessary to enter the joy of heaven.

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2013-2015
defined.quote: All Christians in any state or walk of life are called to the fullness of Christian life and to the perfection of charity.

positions.statement: All are called to perfect charity in this life; those who die in grace but not yet fully purified are cleansed after death before entering heaven.
positions.mark: The passage says those who are saved but not yet wholly holy at death are cleansed after death.
positions.first_defined: Councils of Florence (1439) and Trent (1563), as cited in Catechism 1031

questions.question: After the incarnation, is Christ one nature, or two natures in one person, and how is the union to be stated?
shared_ground: Christ is truly God and truly man (all three positions)
The union is without confusion or change (all three)
Christ is one Lord and Son, worshipped with a single worship
Christ is consubstantial with the Father and with us
'Fully God and fully man' without saying 'one nature' or 'two natures'

positions.name: Two natures in one person (Chalcedon)

defined.source: Council of Chalcedon, Definition of the Faith (451)
defined.quote: acknowledged in two natures which undergo no confusion, no change, no division, no separation

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 467 (quoting Chalcedon)
defined.quote: Following the holy Fathers, we unanimously teach and confess one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: the same perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity

defined.source: Augsburg Confession (1530)
defined.quote: so that there are two natures, the divine and the human, inseparably enjoined in one Person

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith (1646)
defined.quote: So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, the Godhead and the manhood, were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion.

defined.source: Second London Baptist Confession (1689), ch. 8
defined.quote: so that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles (1571)
defined.quote: so that two whole and perfect Natures, that is to say, the Godhead and Manhood, were joined together in one Person, never to be divided

defined.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: so that two whole and perfect natures, that is to say, the Godhead and Manhood, were joined together in one person, never to be divided

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
defined.quote: The Lord Jesus Christ, as to His divine and eternal nature, is the proper and only Begotten of the Father, but as to His human nature, He is the proper Son of Man.

positions.statement: After the union Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, each keeping its own properties, without confusion, change, division or separation.
positions.mark: The passage says Christ is in two natures after the union, concurring in one person and one hypostasis (subsistence).
positions.first_defined: Tome of Leo (449); Council of Chalcedon, Definition of the Faith (451)

positions.name: One incarnate nature of God the Word (miaphysite)

defined.source: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, The Faith of the Church (text by V. C. Samuel, 1970)
defined.quote: On this ground the Church of Ethiopia, with the other Oriental Orthodox Churches, affirms that Jesus Christ is not two natures, but one incarnate nature of God the Word.

defined.source: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, The Faith of the Church (text by V. C. Samuel, 1970)
defined.quote: The Church of Ethiopia, with the other Oriental Orthodox Churches, has refused to accept the Chalcedonian Definition of the Faith with the affirmation that Christ is "made known in two natures."

defined.source: CopticChurch.net, Theology (summary of Pope Shenouda III, The Nature of Christ)
defined.quote: His Divine nature is one with his human nature yet without mingling, confusion or alteration; a complete Hypostatic Union.

defined.source: Armenian Apostolic Church, Pontifical Legation of Western Europe, Faith
defined.quote: In the 5th century the Armenian Church did not accept the Council of Chalcedon in 451. In 506 at the Dvin Council, the Armenian Church formulated an official response to Chalcedon defending its Christology.

positions.statement: God the Word united manhood to himself so that Christ is one incarnate nature of God the Word, Godhead and manhood continuing in him without mixture, confusion or change; 'two natures' is not said after the union.
positions.mark: The passage says that after the union Christ is one nature of God the Word incarnate, or refuses 'two natures' after the union while denying any mixture.
positions.first_defined: Cyril of Alexandria's 'one nature of God the Word incarnate' (letters to Succensus, c. 433); refusal of Chalcedon by the non-Chalcedonian churches after 451; Armenian Council of Dvin (506)

positions.name: Two natures, each with its own qnoma, in one person (Church of the East)

defined.source: Assyrian Church of the East, Diocese of California, FAQ
defined.quote: The Church is diaphysite, and thus holds two natures in Christ—the Godhead or divine, and the human—which are preserved in their respective 'qnome', or substances. The two natures are united in the one Person of Filiation of the Son of God.

defined.source: Common Christological Declaration, Catholic Church and Assyrian Church of the East (1994)
defined.quote: In him has been preserved the difference of the natures of divinity and humanity, with all their properties, faculties and operations.

positions.statement: Christ's Godhead and manhood each remain a complete nature with its own qnoma (concrete individual reality), united in the one person (parsopa) of the Son; the Church of the East does not speak of one hypostasis for the union.
positions.mark: The passage says each nature in Christ keeps its own concrete subsistence (qnoma or hypostasis) and that the two are united in one person (prosopon or parsopa).

questions.question: Will Christ reign on earth for a thousand years after he returns (Revelation 20), or is the thousand years the present age?
shared_ground: Christ will return visibly in glory
The dead will be raised and all will be judged
Christ reigns now at the Father's right hand
Revelation 20 quoted without saying when the thousand years fall

positions.name: Christ returns before a thousand-year reign on earth

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
defined.quote: The second coming of Christ includes the rapture of the saints, which is our blessed hope, followed by the visible return of Christ with His saints to reign on earth for one thousand years.

defined.source: Church of God (Cleveland, TN), Declaration of Faith
defined.quote: In the premillennial second coming of Jesus. First, to resurrect the righteous dead and to catch away the living saints to Him in the air. Second, to reign on the earth a thousand years.

defined.source: International Pentecostal Holiness Church, Articles of Faith
defined.quote: We believe in the imminent, personal, premillennial second coming of our Lord Jesus Christ

positions.statement: Christ will return before a thousand-year reign on earth, raising the righteous first; the last judgment follows the thousand years.
positions.mark: The passage says Christ, or the saints with him, will reign on earth for a thousand years after his coming and a first resurrection, before the end.
positions.first_defined: No early creed defines it; taught by Papias, Justin (Dialogue 80-81) and Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.32-36). Modern confessional form: AG Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916)

positions.name: The thousand years is the present age

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 676
defined.quote: the Church has rejected even modified forms of this falsification of the kingdom to come under the name of millenarianism

defined.source: Augsburg Confession, Article XVII (1530), condemning the view
defined.quote: They condemn also others who are now spreading … that before the resurrection of the dead the godly shall take possession of the kingdom of the world, the ungodly being everywhere suppressed.

defined.source: Second Helvetic Confession, Chapter XI (1566), condemning the view
defined.quote: We further condemn … that there will be a golden age on earth before the Day of Judgment

positions.statement: There is no earthly thousand-year reign after Christ's return; the thousand years of Revelation 20 is Christ's present reign with his saints, ended by one return, one general resurrection and one judgment.
positions.mark: The passage says the thousand years is the present age or the Church's present reign, or rejects any earthly golden age of the saints either before or after Christ's return.
positions.first_defined: Augustine, City of God 20.7-9 (c. 426), for the reading; condemnations of an earthly kingdom in Augsburg XVII (1530), Second Helvetic XI (1566), Catechism 676 (1992)

positions.name: Christ returns after a golden age of the gospel

defined.source: Savoy Declaration of Faith and Order (1658)
defined.quote: we expect that in the latter days, antichrist being destroyed, the Jews called, and the adversaries of the kingdom of his dear Son broken, the churches of Christ being enlarged, and edified through a free and plentiful communication of light and grace, shall enjoy in this world a more quiet, peaceable and glorious condition than they have enjoyed.

positions.statement: Before Christ returns, the gospel will spread so widely that the Church enjoys a long age of peace and righteousness on earth; Christ returns after it.
positions.mark: The passage says that before Christ's return the Church will triumph through the gospel and enjoy a long earthly age of peace and righteousness.
positions.first_defined: Savoy Declaration 26.5 (1658, Congregationalist), in a mild form
